newsitem.title: ITALY: Germans fear Italy would destabilise euro - adviser.
newsitem.headline: Germans fear Italy would destabilise euro - adviser.

text.p: Ordinary Germans fear Italy will import instability into a single European currency if it takes part in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Horst Siebert, an economic adviser to the German government, was quoted on Monday as saying.

He also questioned in an interview with Italian daily Il Corriere della Sera whether Italy would be able to meet certain key economic criteria required for joining EMU at its 1999 start without "window dressing" its accounts.
Siebert, who is president of the Kiel Institute of World Economics, said the principle of stability was fundamental to the collective German psyche after 50 years of low inflation and a strong mark.
He noted that in the same period Italy had seen wide price and lira fluctuations.
"The average citizen perceives a political and economic instability and is worried that with the entrance of Italy these phenomena could be 'imported' into the euro," he said.
He noted no one had actually said Italy could not join, adding: "we will see in 1998 when the evaluation is made."
"It's just that, exactly because of this tradition which characterises it, Italy cannot expect to have special treatment.

"And therefore it really has to ask itself above all if it is capable of respecting the Maastricht criteria. In particular whether it can reach the three percent deficit to gross domestic product ratio this year, going from the 7.4 percent of 1996 without accounting tricks," he said.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has insisted Italy is putting its finances in order to join EMU.
He has spent the past week emphasising what he sees as Italian fitness for a single currency amid persistent talk of mounting pressure in Germany to delay entry for Italy and Spain.
Asked whether speculation of a German drive to keep Italy and Spain out of EMU was also related to domestic German politics, Siebert replied:
"It's possible that the 1998 election date is pushing the opposition to harness public concern about Italy's entrance.
"But the fundamental point is still about respecting the parameters regarding deficit, debt, inflation, interest rates and exchange rate stability.
